Biomimicry Principles in Architecture for Promoting Healthy Buildings:
An Analysis of Relevant Literatures
Gourav Dey
Faculty of Architecture, Chulalongkorn University, Bangkok, Thailand
Abstract
Architecture is no stranger to challenges, and the tropical regions have their own share due to
urbanization and climate change. High temperatures plus humidity and solar radiation that can be likened to
a prickling pain all stand against the promotion of human comfort through architectural designs that take into
account traditional approaches— they fail at countering these factors. This research is about applying biological
imitation strategies in building design to see wellness fostered in the light of nature’s adaptive and efficient
capabilities, aiming at extracting good practices from biological models for tropical architecture. The approach
includes reviews of literature touching on various issues ranging from thermal comfort to daylighting, ventilation,
and moisture management, among others— through case studies. Even as we acknowledge the promise that
biomimetic innovations hold, we do not turn a blind eye on their limitations: they should integrate culture, be
accepted by communities, come about through collaboration between architects (engineers environmentalists’
sociologists), others working with local people. Some notable examples include passive cooling systems
(inspired by termite mounds) or self-cleaning surfaces (imitating lotus leaves) or spatial designs like those
receiving light and air openings from rainforest canopies' tiered structure— but these also pose technological
cultural challenges that act as barriers unless mitigated; in such case only can their full potential be realized.
Biomimetic architecture, particularly useful for architects working in tropical zones where environmental factors
dominate design considerations and therefore the primary use of those principles, is also presented as a
response. It paves way for a creative leap: buildings developed through this approach not only stand as
sustainable structures but additionally support user comfortability. The significance of using biomimicry in
achieving healthy built environments is discussed in this paper to highlight how nature-based design promotes
both occupant wellness and energy conservation. We look at biomimetic design principles alongside successful
case studies that give practical lessons on what to implement when dealing with biomimetic architecture,
providing an insight on what should be expected as outcomes from such projects.
Keywords
Biomimicry Architecture, Healthy Building, Indoor environment, Sustainability, well-being requirements; well-
being
1 | J A R S

1. Introduction
The widely recognized definition of health was proposed by the World Health Organization in
1946("CONSTITUTION OF THE WORLD HEALTH ORGANIZATION," 1946) which described health as being
"a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity."
This definition has come under fire for being utopian, idealistic, outdated; it is challenging to sustain such a
state in today's imperfect society where there are many other aspects to consider apart from just the absence
of disease(Misselbrook, 2014). Not only is the absence of disease enough but also many other things. Health
— that elusive trifecta of physical, mental and emotional well-being — is heavily influenced by our
surroundings. On one end of the spectrum lies the optimal built environment: a place that keeps us vibrant,
inspired, and connected. Yet, at the other end looms the insidious impact of poorly constructed spaces—
fostering feelings of desolation, boredom, even trapping us in a cycle of despair. So, remember when we talk
about staying healthy in such spaces, we aren't only referring to pumping iron at a gymnasium. It's also those
social interactions easily facilitated when spaces are well designed; they’re as important for our health as any
amount of physical activity we can muster inside these walls(Christoforou et al., 2024).
The concept of healthy building design is crucial for enhancing the well-being of occupants by focusing on
physical, psychological, and social aspects of health. Research has demonstrated that the physical
environment, including indoor air quality (IAQ), thermal comfort, and acoustics, plays a significant role in the
physical health of individuals residing or working within these spaces. In addition to physical needs, the
psychological well-being of occupants is also a priority, with factors such as lighting, color schemes, and views
significantly impacting mental health(Liu et al., 2023). Moreover, healthy building design extends beyond the
individual, emphasizing the importance of social needs and resources, which are integral to creating a
supportive and health-promoting environment(Liu et al., 2023). The design of a building is not merely the
arrangement of stones and mortar: it is an art. It is this complete way of looking at health needs, including the
physical environmental factors, the psychological comfort, social well-being all together; to be able to deliver
a truly healthy place for people who live or work in that space. But creating such spaces has never been more
crucial than it is now— society continues to push out masses onto aware lines regarding healthy design due
largely to an increasing number that have come into existence over recent years, paying attention at last to
this significant facet of architecture and construction: healthy buildings.
“Wellbeing” has been defined in different ways. Watson described wellbeing as embodying “thinking, feeling
and functioning”(Watson, 2018). It has also been described as a byproduct of satisfying Maslow’s hierarchy of
needs, a subjective result of contextual comparison, and the freedom to flourish(Fleuret, 2007). Integrative
health fosters wellbeing through careful consideration of all these aspects at the individual, social and
environmental levels.
As a culture, it is estimated that Americans spend over ninety percent of their time indoors (Razjouyan et al.,
2020). As we continue to spend most of our time indoors, it is important to design spaces to support health
2 | J A R S

and prevent disease. This is especially true for those spaces in which we live and work. Health can be
considered as one of the four fundamental aspects (namely safety, comfort, convenience, and health) that
contribute to a building's functionality, specifically designed to cater to the needs of humans (Chairiyah, 2023).
Happiness by Design proposes a path to salient happiness as a precursor to Dolan et al.’s (Dolan et al., 2016)
seven SALIENT elements of design, which account for the impact of sound, air, light, image, ergonomics,
nature and tint on wellbeing (Dolan, 2014; Dolan et al., 2016). Among other contributions, The Shaping of Us
adds layout, cohesion, energy, and more artistic elements of design to this list (Bernheimer, 2019). In the
Seven Core Areas of Integrative Health
Sleep Resilience Environment Movement Relationship Spirituality Nutrition
current article’s proposed construct, elements of built environment design and operation, which support
integrative health and wellbeing, are overlaid on the seven core areas or domains of integrative health: sleep,
resilience, environment, movement, relationships, spirituality, and nutrition(Engineer et al., 2021).
The concept of biomimicry gained renewed popularity through the efforts of biologist Janine Benyus, and its
application in the field of architecture was spearheaded by renowned architects Nicholas Grimshaw, Mick
Pearce, Norman Foster, and Michael Pawlyn. Biomimicry in architecture embraces the idea of drawing
inspiration from nature and seamlessly integrating it into the design process, encompassing the form, function,
and system of the built environment(Janine_Benyus).
The integration of biomimetic design into the architectural landscape offers a multifaceted approach to
enhancing human health and well-being. By mimicking natural patterns and systems, these designs not only
aim to create aesthetically pleasing environments but also to foster physical and mental health benefits for
individuals. For instance, such designs prioritize the use of natural light and the inclusion of plant life within
office spaces, which has been shown to result in higher levels of job satisfaction and reduced strain among
employees. This approach aligns with the broader objectives of biomimetic design to generate spaces that are
not only sustainable but also conducive to promoting healthier lifestyles. The accessibility to green spaces, a
core principle of biomimetic architecture, encourages physical activity among building occupants, thereby
contributing to their overall health and well-being. Furthermore, the emphasis on creating environments that
regulate circadian rhythms underscores the commitment of biomimetic design to the physical health of
individuals, enhancing the quality of sleep and, by extension, their general health(Hower et al., 2018). This
holistic perspective on design demonstrates how biomimicry can bridge the gap between sustainable
architecture and the promotion of health, underlining the potential of such approaches to transform built
environments into spaces that nurture both the planet and its inhabitants.
3 | J A R S

This paper outlines the revolutionary potential of imitating nature when designing buildings. Architectural design
that emulates nature's strategies not only results in eco-friendly structures but also has a positive impact on
the people who use them. The primary theme of this study is an investigation into biomimicry's impact on
architectural practice, emphasizing its role in building performance and aesthetics, as well as sustainability.
We introduce the notion of architects being at the frontier line where they have to make decisions aiming at
creating more harmony between built environments and nature; there are implications to their choices based
on resilience and creativity from mimicking natural systems for healthy coexistence. Although we promote
positive aspects that come with adoption of biomimicry principles within architecture such as awareness about
limitations due to biases— we also call upon continued research development efforts through this discipline
given future negative effects it can pose towards occupants living in those buildings contributing further still
towards environmentally sustainable actions emerging out from local communities, supporting individuals
involved directly or indirectly with these places.
1.1. Architecture and Health
The architecture profession has an important part to play in the puzzle to improve the healthiness of buildings.
The Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) Code of Professional Conduct includes a public interest principle
to protect the wellbeing of the general public and gives priority to this over all other principles (RIBA Code of
Professional Conduct May 2019, 2019). Whilst there are many other stakeholders involved, including
engineers, accountants, clients, users, consultants, town planners as well as statutory legislation and other
building regulations, it is the architecture profession which invariably has the key role integrating the inputs
from this network into a comprehensive and buildable reality. There are a number of challenges facing the
implementation of healthier buildings by the architecture profession. First is a lack of knowledge; much more
research is required on the complex inter-relationships between built environment factors and their impact on
human health. Whilst there are already many existing isolated studies on individual health indicators, more
needs to be known about them in combination. Secondly, the architecture profession is not currently required
to learn about human health as part of its mandated educational curriculum. This might seem surprising, but
at present, none of the professional institutions of architecture specifically requires a knowledge of health
and/or wellbeing (Rice, 2019). This extends to a lack of understanding of population-level approaches and
working to address health inequalities which by comparison are integral to public health practice (Good-Public-
Health-Practice-Framework, 2016). A paradigm shift in the profession is required in order to address this
aspect. Thirdly, the rise of non-communicable diseases is associated with contemporary “lifestyles”; these are
highly complex interrelationships that combine aspects of the built environment with socio-cultural factors,
legislation, behavioral patterns, advertising, social media and economics. The drivers of non-communicable
diseases are inbuilt into the design DNA of many contemporary cities (Rice & Drane, 2020). Lastly, there are
often financial limitations that impinge on the inclusion of healthy design features as “too expensive or costly”.
The financial costs of ill-health are already known, for example days lost due to absenteeism at work or the
cost to health services treating these illnesses and run into the billions of pounds/dollars/euros (Rice & Drane,
4 | J A R S

2020). However, these costs have not yet found their way upstream; poor design decisions are made with the
full knowledge that they may cause health problems later on, but there is no mechanism available yet to
enable greater costs to be allocated upstream.
1.2. Biomimicry principles
Biomimicry principles offer a revolutionary approach to architecture, aiming to emulate nature's efficiency and
sustainability in building design. By drawing inspiration from natural systems and processes, biomimetic
architecture seeks to create structures that are not only environmentally friendly but also innovative and
aesthetically pleasing. One of the fundamental goals of biomimicry in architecture is to enhance the built
environment's capacity for regenerating local ecosystems and increasing resilience(Zari, 2007). This approach
involves applying nature's energy-saving processes and closed loops with minimal waste to architectural
design, leading to more efficient and sustainable buildings. Additionally, biomimicry principles can be utilized
to develop materials that are stronger, tougher, self-assembling, and self-healing, contributing to the creation
of durable and resilient structures(Verbrugghe et al., 2023). By integrating biomimicry into architectural
practices, designers can explore a wide range of ideas and solutions that not only meet human requirements
but also align with nature's wisdom, fostering harmony between the built environment and the natural world.
Ultimately, the application of biomimicry principles in architecture holds the promise of transforming the industry
towards more environmentally conscious and ecologically beneficial practices. According to Biomimicry 3.8
(2021), the six major biomimicry principles are as follows:
(i) Resource (material and energy) efficiency
(ii) Evolution for survival
(iii) Adapting to changing conditions
(iv) Integrating development with growth
(v) Being locally attuned and responsive
(vi) Using life-friendly chemistry
Biomimicry in architecture offers a unique approach to design that not only benefits the environment but also
enhances human well-being. By looking to nature as a mentor, architects can unlock extraordinary solutions
to complex design challenges, leading to the creation of a regenerative world where architecture and nature
seamlessly converge. Through biomimicry, architects, interior designers, and construction companies can
develop sustainable heating, cooling, lighting, and water management systems by observing the efficient
energy and resource management strategies employed by plants, animals, and ecosystems. By incorporating
biomimicry strategies into projects, professionals in the field can stay ahead of the market, create sustainable
designs, improve building performance, enhance aesthetics, and contribute to a more sustainable built
environment. The interdisciplinary nature of biomimicry in architecture brings together biologists, designers,
engineers, and other experts to study and apply principles from nature, fostering innovative and sustainable
5 | J A R S

outcomes. Biomimicry in architecture is a relatively new approach that holds great potential for the future of
sustainable design. This approach has gained popularity in recent years as professionals recognize the
importance of creating sustainable buildings and infrastructure. The principles of biomimicry in architecture
have been developed to guide the design process toward creating structures that are more in tune with the
natural world. Another commonly cited three key principles of biomimicry are:
Nature as Model: Studying nature's models and imitating or
taking inspiration from its designs and processes to solve
human problems.
Nature as Measure: Using an ecological standard to judge
the sustainability of our innovations.
Nature as Mentor: Observing and valuing nature's operating
instructions.
These principles were outlined by Janine Benyus, one of the
founders of the field of biomimicry. They guide the practice
of learning from and emulating nature's successful strategies
Fig: Elements of Biomimicry (AI Generated)
and solutions through the study of natural forms, processes, and ecosystems to develop more sustainable and
efficient designs, materials, and systems(Janine_Benyus).
Biomimicry, a practice that involves imitating natural systems and processes to design more sustainable and
efficient structures, has gained significant attention in the realm of architecture and sustainable design. By
drawing inspiration from nature, architects can create buildings that are better suited to their environments,
leading to structures with a lower ecological footprint and a reduced impact on the environment. Biomimicry
architecture not only helps in designing structures that are better adapted to local conditions but also promotes
the efficient use of resources such as energy, water, and materials by emulating the systems found in nature.
Through biomimicry practices, architects can enhance the lives of building occupants while minimizing the
negative effects on the natural world, thus contributing to sustainable design practices. Additionally, biomimicry
has the potential to transform urban spaces and societal systems by reimagining food production, waste
management, community-building, and education, as showcased by Yaniv Peer's Mobius Project. This
approach not only offers practical insights for industry professionals but also presents a promising direction
for future research in sustainable design practices. By embracing biomimicry and its principles, architects can
not only create more sustainable buildings but also foster a deeper connection between humans and nature,
ultimately contributing to the regeneration of ecosystems and the achievement of sustainable designs.
6 | J A R S

There are five potential dimensions to biomimicry: (1) how the design mimics the look and form of an
ecosystem, (2) how it mimics the material of an ecosystem, (3) how it mimics the way that the ecosystem is
being constructed, (4) how the ecosystem works (process) and (5) what the ecosystem is capable of doing
(function). These levels are often used as benchmarks for architects to employ bio-mimicry principles in design
and architecture approaches and create sustainable, efficient, and environmentally sound buildings(Jamei &
Vrcelj, 2021).
2. Literature Review
Existing research on healthy buildings were reviewed and analyzed systematically to identify current knowledge
gaps and determine future research directions. A literature review was conducted online via Chula library
website across various databases including MDPI, ScienceDirect, Scopus, Research Gate, Taylor & Francis,
JARS but not limited to Existing research on healthy buildings were reviewed and analyzed systematically to
identify current knowledge gaps and determine future research directions. Specifically, the first step was data
collection, which identified the source and number of publications. The second step was data analysis.
This research method uses the content analysis method, which is qualitative descriptive. The content analysis
includes the process of unitization, categorization, codification, inference and verification. The study analyzed
various Biomimicry Architecture literature related to Healthy Building and Healthy Building criteria. Content
analysis is carried out by uniting writings with keywords according to health, healthy building, and healthy
building criteria such as Good Air Conditioning System, Material Health Control, Lighting and Views, Noise
Control, Good Building Plan, Water Quality, and Environmental Sustainability Contributes. After uniting the
related words, sentences and paragraphs in the biomimicry architectural literature, they are grouped and
codified based on their characters' similarities. The codification results are two groups: Biomimicry in
Architecture to support human health and the environment and Biomimicry in Architecture close to Healthy
Environment. After being codified, an abstraction was carried out to explain the two categories. A date range
of the years 2000-2024 was established by the relevancy of results as well as limitations of the search
databases. The inclusion criteria for these articles consisted of at least one or more built environment theme
or finding connected to one or more of the seven domains of integrative health(AlAli et al., 2023).
2.1. The Nature of Nature
Nature is indeed a big idea that can be looked at in many ways. At its heart, it deals with basic queries on
what the essence of nature is made up of— how it came about and how it functions. Nature implies the quality
and totality of the ecosphere or even the universe itself. In this wide scope, it speaks to physical laws, elements
and life phenomena in their wholeness as constituents of the living world order(Sala, 2020) .
7 | J A R S

Biomimicry is a design approach that draws inspiration from nature's ingenuity and applies its principles and
strategies to solve human challenges. In the realm of architectural design, biomimicry has emerged as a
significant concept, offering innovative solutions that are both sustainable and efficient. Here are several ways
exploring the significance of biomimicry in architectural design:
2.1.1. Embracing Nature's Wisdom
Biomimicry in architecture encourages designers to observe and emulate nature's time-tested patterns and
systems. Over billions of years, nature has evolved intricate designs that are optimized for efficient use of
resources, energy conservation, and structural resilience. By studying and mimicking these natural blueprints,
architects can create buildings that are not only aesthetically pleasing but also highly functional and
environmentally responsive.
There are a number of living ecosystem examples that are highly energy efficient. They serve as great
inspiration for how humans can strive to be less reliant on fossil fuels biomimicry. It provides great potentials
for learning from nature and developing solutions that result in a reduced level of energy consumption. Four
principles are used in biomimicry to reduce the overall energy consumption; 1. Decreasing the demand, 2.
Identifying unlimited sources of energies; 3. Sustainable energy distributing systems, and 4. Decreasing the
non-toxic flows compatible with wide range of system(Omer, 2008).
2.1.2. Sustainable Design Strategies
One of the most significant contributions of biomimicry to architectural design is its emphasis on sustainability.
Nature operates in a closed-loop system, where waste is minimized, and resources are constantly recycled.
Architects can learn from this principle by designing buildings that are energy-efficient, utilize renewable
materials, and seamlessly integrate with their surroundings. Biomimetic strategies such as passive cooling,
natural ventilation, and water harvesting can significantly reduce a building's environmental impact. Chen Lin
et all conducted research on carbon emissions, policies, models, and sustainable materials like biochar,
bioplastic, agricultural waste, animal wool, ash, and self-healing concrete. This research drew from national
policy frameworks and technology roadmaps of the United States, Japan, China, and the European Union,
providing valuable insights into reducing carbon footprints (Chen et al., 2023).
2.1.3. Structural Optimization
Nature's designs are not only beautiful but also remarkably efficient and resilient. Biomimicry offers architects
insights into optimizing building structures by studying the strength, flexibility, and load-bearing capabilities of
natural forms. For instance, the intricate patterns found in honeycomb structures or the branching patterns of

Fig. Honeycomb (left) and the sandwich structure's schematic view (right) (Source: https://en.wiki
edia.org/wiki/Sandwich-structured_composite).
trees can inspire lightweight yet robust architectural designs that consume fewer resources while maintaining
structural integrity.
Honeycomb is a live structure that inspired many structural engineering projects(Peterson, 2009). One of the
well-known applications is the use of honeycomb cell for sandwich construction, an innovation highly
appreciated in structural engineering. The two components of the sandwich are glued strongly using adhesive
so that they work as a single unit with high rigidity in both torsion and bending.
2.1.4. Adaptive and Responsive Designs
Another significant aspect of biomimicry in architecture is the creation of adaptive and responsive designs.
Nature's systems are dynamic and capable of responding to changing environmental conditions(Faragalla &
Asadi, 2022). Architects can mimic this adaptability by incorporating kinetic elements, smart materials, and
responsive technologies into their designs. Buildings that can adjust their orientation, shading, or ventilation
systems in response to external factors like sunlight, wind, and temperature can significantly improve energy
efficiency and occupant comfort. South Korea’s Thematic Pavilion is an example of an integrated self-shaded
device. It is inspired by a South African flower and has a movable 90-degree flap. The main use of the principle
is solar shading with minimized view obstruction when cloudy weather and full protection from the sun when
sun(Gruber & Jeronimidis, 2012)
2.1.5. Fostering Biophilic Connections
Biomimicry in architecture also promotes biophilic design. The development of biophilic design as a concept
used in the building industry is primarily aimed at enhancing the occupants' connection with nature, typically
achieved through direct nature, indirect nature, and space and place conditions. The approach focuses on
health and well-being("A STUDY ON PRESENCE OF BIOPHILIC,").
Biomimicry offers a rich source of inspiration and innovative solutions for architectural design. By embracing
nature's principles and strategies, architects can create buildings that are not only aesthetically stunning but
also highly functional, sustainable, and harmonious with the environment. Biomimicry represents a paradigm
shift towards a more holistic and nature-centric approach to design, one that recognizes the invaluable wisdom
9 | J A R S

found in the natural world. Additionally, it is worth noting that most functional mimicries originated from insects
and plants at a micro- and nanoscale level(Jamei & Vrcelj, 2021).
2.2. Healthy Building Criteria
Many metrics, including IAQ, temperature, humidity, and lighting, contribute to a healthy building.
Understanding these metrics will help ensure that the buildings do not negatively impact occupants, workers,
or surrounding environment. The more commonly cited set of criteria comes from the WELL Building Standard,
developed by the International WELL Building Institute (IWBI)(Tan & Rahman, 2023). The seven concepts of
the WELL Building Standard are: Air, Water, Nourishment, Light, Fitness, Comfort, Mind. These concepts
cover aspects like air and water quality, access to healthy foods, adequate lighting and views, opportunities
for physical activity, thermal and acoustic comfort, and support for mental and emotional health.
Another seven criteria for healthy buildings are also based on the WELL criteria that are compared below.
(1) Good Air Conditioning Systems, (2) Material Health Control, (3) Lighting and Views, (4) Noise Control,
(5) Good Building Plan, (6) Water Quality, and (7) Environmental Sustainability Contributes. (Chairiyah, 2023)
Criteria for Healthy Buildings WELL Building Standard Concepts
1. Good Air Conditioning Systems Air
2. Material Health Control Water
3. Lighting and Views Nourishment
4. Noise Control Light
5. Good Building Plan Fitness
6. Water Quality Comfort
7. Environmental Sustainability Mind
a. Good Air Conditioning Systems
Proper ventilation and air conditioning is crucial for maintaining indoor air quality. According to the
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), indoor air can be 2-5 times more polluted than outdoor air. HVAC
systems should include air filters (MERV 13 or higher as recommended by ASHRAE) to remove particulate
matter, and may use technologies like UV lights or bipolar ionization to reduce biological and chemical
pollutants(Ottney, 1993). Controlling temperature (68-75°F) and humidity (30-60% RH) is also important for
occupant comfort and preventing mold growth(Wu & Wong, 2022).
10 | J A R S

b. Material Health Control
Building materials can off-gas volatile organic compounds (VOCs) like formaldehyde which are linked to
respiratory issues and cancer risks. The WELL Building Standard restricts volatile organic compound (VOC)
levels and prohibits materials containing lead, asbestos and certain flame retardants. LEED v4 also has
requirements for low-emitting materials. Elastic-tensile biomaterials and hard rigid biomaterials are the two
primary classes of biomaterials. Protein is the primary component of tensile materials, which includes. The
protein is combined with minerals (mainly calcium or silicon) to form stiff biological materials(Al-Ketan et al.,
2022). The instances demonstrate that the utilization of natural materials does not lead to performance
degradation and, in fact, can be highly advantageous. The application of the discovery into structural
engineering is impeded by one major issue: most bio-materials found in nature are not mass producible and
have low durability(Jamei & Vrcelj, 2021).
c. Lighting and Views
Lighting significantly influences human well-being and quality of life. The importance of lighting in buildings
was underscored by Tado Ando and Le Corbusier as they described its effect on us through three ways:
radiation that affects our vision; systems and our circadian system(Boyce, 2010). Access to daylight and views
to the outdoors can improve mood, focus and sleep quality according to studies. The WELL Standard requires
regularly occupied spaces have adequate daylight (300-3000 lux) and views (direct line of sight to outdoors
from 75% of spaces)(Raslan & Saeed, 2023). Appropriate artificial lighting levels (300-500 lux) and circadian
lighting design is also important.
d. Acoustic Comfort
Excessive noise can increase stress and negatively impact sleep and cognitive performance. The WELL
Standard requires meeting certain noise level criteria (35-50 dBA) depending on space type. Experiments in
controlled environments reveal green walls' considerable promise as an acoustic insulator for architectural
structures and that Rw15 dB and a 0.40 can be delivered with ease(Azkorra et al., 2015).
e. Good Building Plan
A good building plan that prioritizes health incorporates various elements to ensure the well-being of its
occupants. Such a plan, based on the 9 Foundations of a Healthy Building as identified by experts from the
Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. These are- Ventilation, Air Quality, Thermal Health, Moisture, Dust
and Pests, Safety and Security, Water Quality, Noise, Lighting and Views.
f. Water Quality
Clean potable water is essential for hydration and avoiding waterborne illnesses. WELL and other standards
require periodic water quality testing for contaminants like lead, microbes and disinfection byproducts and may
specify water treatment methods.
11 | J A R S

g. Environmental Sustainability Contributes
Green Building strategies like energy/water efficiency, , renewable energy, stormwater management and waste
reduction can reduce environmental impacts which indirectly benefit occupant health by reducing pollution
exposure.
3. Case studies
The integration of biomimicry principles in architecture presents a promising avenue for redefining building
design practices towards enhanced sustainability and efficiency. The analysis of relevant literature underscores
the transformative potential of emulating nature's ingenious designs in architectural solutions, with a focus on
conservation of natural resources, mitigation of global warming, and promotion of biodiversity. By drawing
inspiration from nature's energy-saving processes and closed loops, biomimetic architecture offers a pathway
towards creating buildings that are not only environmentally friendly but also innovative and aesthetically
pleasing. Moreover, the fundamental goal of biomimicry in architecture to enhance regenerative capacities of
the built environment and increase resilience underscores the significance of incorporating these principles in
building design. The multifaceted advantages offered by biomimicry principles extend beyond aesthetics to
encompass substantial environmental benefits, including the development of materials that are stronger, self-
assembling, and self-healing, contributing to the creation of durable and resilient structures. The implications
of integrating biomimicry in architecture hold immense potential for shaping a more sustainable and
environmentally conscious built environment, emphasizing the importance of continued research and
application in advancing the field towards a greener future.
3.1. The Bullitt Center, Seattle, USA
Image Source: https://www.voanews.com/a/seattles-bullitt-center-a-green-building-inspiring
visitors/4759826.html
Bullitt Center: an office building that's as sustainable as they come. The structure was completed in 2013 and
was designed by the Miller Hull Partnership to meet the challenging Living Building Challenge— one of the
most rigorous green certifications. It's heralded as one of the greenest commercial buildings globally since it
12 | J A R S

produces all its energy from solar panels and isn't connected to any grid for energy or water; including
composting toilets plus a rainwater harvesting system, among others. These allow it to function with net zero
energy and water consumption annually. During construction, recycled materials were used along with rapidly
renewable resources like wood so that its environmental impact would be minimized even before completion.
Natural daylighting and ventilation are maximized while energy-efficient heating and cooling systems are
provided in a building that serves as an office space for environmental organizations— a living example of
what can be achieved through sustainable design and operation for mid-rise commercial structures(Homchick
Crowe, 2019).
3.2. Bangkok Tree House (Bangkok, Thailand)
The Bangkok Tree House in Bangkok, Thailand, is an eco-friendly resort designed by architect Jirayu
Tulyanond. The resort doesn't just boast about its eco-friendly initiatives; it showcases them proudly. Through
passive sustainable design, they make use of elements like solar and wind energy, rainwater harvesting
systems, and even solar cookers. Construction materials echo the same sentiment with reclaimed wood and
bamboo taking center stage. It was all completed in 2023 as part of a residential project known for prioritizing
green spaces — including trees — as primary users. Located right at the city center, the Bangkok Tree House
is easily reachable through excellent bicycle paths that take visitor through this green oasis. So even though
the visitor staying in the midst of nature's lap, they still find themself well connected to urban conveniences all
while enjoying a quiet stay devoid of any environmental guilt.
.
Image Source: https://www.bangkoktreehouse.com/
This eco-friendly retreat in urban Bangkok is found near the Chao Praya River. This place keeps visitors
distant from the city's hustle and bustle, surrounded by a peaceful atmosphere. The resort comprises just 11
rooms, each sprawling over three levels; but what catches the eye is the 'view with a room'— an open-air
'nest' perched 20 feet above ground level that presents breathtaking views around. Demonstrating sustainable
passive design, the Bangkok Tree House uses solar and wind power, solar cookers, rainwater harvesting

3.3. The EDITT Tower (Singapore)
The EDITT Tower located in Singapore showcases a number of biomimetic design principles that take
inspiration from nature. The organic form of the tower — twisted and spiraled — draws parallels with DNA
helices or seashells which grow through rotational, helical patterns; mimicking such structural geometry
enhances strength plus efficiency without additional load-bearing materials. The facade strategy employs dual
layers to emulate protective outer skins found in plant stems or tree bark that offer shading and environmental

protection: an example from nature shows how one layer can do more than one job. The rotation of floors to
provide shading for lower levels demonstrates passive design strategies borrowed from ecosystems where
components work together: it also reduces energy consumption by eliminating need for mechanical cooling
systems. Cross-ventilation is achieved through building porosity and orifice manipulation as a way plants or
animals would channel airflows to regulate temperature; similarly, irregular forms help resist dynamic loads
without compromising visual quality at all points around the building perimeter due to differing orientations—
like those between leaves on a stem or spots on an animal's back. An optimal arrangement of units based on
external views, another free resource- balances daylight penetration while minimizing heat gain during hot
periods (solar access) revealing hidden sources within their environment and fostering good stewardship
among inhabitants toward their local context.
3.4. Pearl River Tower (Guangzhou, China)
The Pearl River Tower in Guangzhou, China takes inspiration from nature's design principles. Its slender and
curved form imitates natural aerodynamic shapes seen in elements like bamboo stems or grass blades —
designed not to fight but flow with wind forces(Frechette, 2008). As plants harness wind power for dispersal
and growth, so does the tower with embedded wind turbines that catch prevailing winds for energy generation.
Termites achieve optimal mound temperatures without mechanical systems; similarly, the tower uses radiant
cooling and heating inspired by termite mounds' natural ventilation. Optimal load distribution without redundant
members as observed in trees’ branches, is echoed within the tower’s structural design. Light-directing panels
guide daylight deep into interior spaces— like compound eyes capture light information or chloroplasts retain
photosynthesis from plant facades. Rainwater runoff isn't wasted but collected and stored on site for reuse
later; a strategy employed by various flora species sustaining themselves within their local ecosystems.

4. The advantages of applying biomimicry in building design
Incorporating biomimicry in building design offers multifaceted advantages that extend beyond mere aesthetics,
encompassing substantial environmental benefits as well. By mimicking nature's ingenious designs, buildings
16 | J A R S

can contribute significantly to conserving natural resources and reducing global warming, while also aiding in
the restoration of natural resources and protection of biodiversity. Biomimetic designs contribute to lower
operating costs in buildings through several mechanisms that enhance efficiency and sustainability. Here are
the key ways in which these designs help reduce costs:
Biomimetic architecture often incorporates natural cooling and heating strategies, reducing reliance on
mechanical systems(Gruber, 2011). For example, buildings that mimic termite mounds for natural ventilation
and temperature regulation can significantly cut down on the use of air conditioning and heating systems,
leading to lower energy consumption and reduced utility bills.
Natural systems are typically less complex and more durable than mechanical systems. Biomimetic designs
that use materials and structures inspired by nature can be more resilient and require less maintenance. For
instance, self-cleaning surfaces inspired by the lotus leaf can reduce the need for frequent cleaning and
maintenance(Finsterwalde, 2011).
Biomimicry encourages the use of materials in a way that mimics the efficiency of natural systems, often
leading to less waste during construction(Al-Ketan et al., 2022). This efficient use of materials can reduce the
overall material costs and waste management expenses.
Biomimetic designs often reduce the need for mechanical heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC)
systems by optimizing natural ventilation and temperature regulation(Webb, 2022). For example, buildings like
the Eastgate Centre in Zimbabwe use natural cooling systems inspired by termite mounds, which significantly
cut down on the energy required for air conditioning. The energy savings from reduced HVAC use can be
substantial, often reducing energy consumption by 30-50% compared to conventional buildings.
By mimicking the resilience of natural systems, biomimetic buildings can be more durable and require fewer
repairs over time(Gruber, 2011). This extends the lifecycle of the building components and reduces the
frequency and cost of replacements.
Enhanced indoor air quality and natural light can improve occupant health and productivity, potentially reducing
costs associated with healthcare and increasing the overall productivity in commercial settings(Al Horr et al.,
2016). Healthier environments also tend to have lower turnover rates and absenteeism.
Many governments and organizations offer incentives for sustainable building practices, including tax
reductions, grants, and rebates. Buildings with biomimetic designs that meet certain environmental standards
may qualify for these incentives, further reducing operational costs.
Buildings with innovative biomimetic designs and improved indoor air quality are often more attractive to
tenants and buyers, leading to higher occupancy rates and potentially higher rental incomes.
These factors combined make biomimetic designs not only environmentally sustainable but also economically
advantageous, particularly in the long term. By reducing the operational demands and enhancing the building's
17 | J A R S

efficiency, biomimetic architecture can lead to substantial cost savings. The unique aesthetic and functional
appeal of biomimetic buildings can also increase property values over time.
5. Discussion: Challenges and Future Directions
Biomimicry within architectural designs can have a significant impact on the quality of air indoors(Bibri &
Krogstie, 2020). In addition to the health of occupants, this approach enables integration of design principles
and materials that take inspiration from natural systems inherently optimized for air purification and control of
humidity, thus promoting environmental balance in totality. The field of biomimicry is indeed fascinating; it is
rapidly evolving with the aim of creating buildings and spaces that are sustainable, efficient, and in harmony
with their natural surroundings. However, such biomimetic solutions are often localized based on specific
climates and contexts which were identified during their inception.
The task of translating these nature-based strategies to different geographical areas can indeed be challenging
due to varying climatic conditions which may necessitate borrowing from various sources or even modifying
the principles themselves.
Biomimetic designs, though highly efficient and sustainable, may be challenging when applied to larger
buildings or urban areas due to their complex nature, which can lead them to be even more costly than
common methods, at least in the short term. The discussion of scalability and cost-benefit of such approaches
is necessary.
In the context of biomimicry, architects have to work closely with engineers, biologists, material scientists and
other professionals so as to comprehensively grasp natures concepts and apply them in building development:
the effective translation of nature's principles into building design and construction. Establishing interdisciplinary
cooperation that promotes sharing knowledge is also very important.
Biomimetic designs are gaining more popularity, thus there is a need for an effective and reliable performance
monitoring and validation that would be able to measure the effects of these strategies on human health,
energy efficiency, and environmental sustainability. This valuable data can then drive the enhancement and
optimization of biomimetic strategies.
Raising the levels of education and awareness about biomimicry principles among architects as well as builders
and even ordinary citizens plays a major role in helping people appreciate such designs. We must introduce
the study of biomimicry into architecture curricula as well as professional training programs so that we can
make these innovative nature-based approaches mainstream.
The establishment of bio-mimic building codes, policies and norms that either provide incentives or make it
obligatory for builders to incorporate the principles of biomimicry into building designs can highly facilitate its
widespread implementation. It will help foster a healthier built environment.

However, despite the complexity of translating biological concepts into architectural designs, let us pledge to
address these challenges and evolve with time on principles regarding biomimicry in architecture— this is the
only way we will unleash the potential to develop buildings that enhance human health and environmental
sustainability through learning from nature's strategies. The lack of proper education and wide understanding
on these principles among architects creates a stumbling block in their adoption; likewise, failure by building
codes and regulations to accommodate some innovative features leads to legal implications.
Cost implications also arise from innovations in biomimicry due to advanced materials and technology—
challenging for production procurement owing to cost, which includes getting such materials may lead some
builders into financial crisis without expecting since they are not guaranteed returns.
Exploring biomimicry further can result in innovative materials and ways, which can be introduced into the
mainstream architectural practices. Teaching biomimicry in schools of architecture can equip students with the
knowledge that their designs should always go hand in hand with nature. It will help to have a bridge between
biologists, architects, and engineers which will lead to more effective solutions in the design process by better
understanding each other's needs. Advocating for changes in building codes is essential as it would support
biometric development; therefore, this could open more opportunities.
Biomimicry stands on the horizon revolutionizing human construction of buildings to make them adaptive and
resilient from components: sustainable biological. By mimicking nature, we can create environments that meet
not only human needs but are also friendly ecosystems where they will find themselves.
6. Conclusion
The idea of biomimicry is very promising in the area of building constructions that are environmentally friendly
and also durable. Instead of just meeting human needs, architects can mimic nature's time-tested design
strategies so as to come up with structures that foster not only the health of their occupants but also the
ecosystems around them. The notion that should be adopted is to let buildings emulate living organisms in all
aspects: this includes self-sufficiency for energy and resources, efficiency like a metabolism, resilience to
changes like an immune system, biodiversity for different functions in such complex systems like an ecosystem.
Biomimicry in architectural design — nurturing healthy indoor spaces. Let's delve into this review that highlights
successful examples of projects such as the Bullitt Center, Bangkok Tree House, EDITT Tower, and Pearl
River Tower that have used nature-inspired approaches to address challenges like air quality and thermal
comfort. Not forgetting daylighting; these projects also take into consideration material health considerations
and design elements from nature due to the diverse requirements of these structures. For biomimicry to thrive
in architecture, it calls for research and knowledge sharing: integration of biomimicry principles into architectural
education and professional development programs would see practitioners easily adopt nature-based
19 | J A R S

approaches as part of their standard practice. Collaboration is key— collaboration between architects,
engineers, biologists, and material scientists will ensure effective implementation of nature's strategies in built
environment projects developed by interdisciplinary teams. The review ensures we capture all essential details
regarding biomimicry in architecture while providing insightful guidance on how best it can be promoted within
this field.
The advancement of biomimicry in architecture is possible by introducing new rules and regulations that
encourage or make it mandatory to use principles of biomimicry. This would result in the creation of
environments that are not only environmentally friendly but also promote well-being. Embracing biomimicry in
architecture means rejecting the usual way of design; instead, take a holistic approach from nature. The
approach recognizes that nature has infinite wisdom — hence, by learning from nature, architects can develop
highly functional systems which are also resilient and prioritize human health as well as ecological
sustainability. By acknowledging that nature holds all the answers we seek, we are empowered to create
systems that work beautifully for all life on earth.
